h: Shabbos Garments Reflect Service in the Divine Palace

p: "And he shall remove his garments, etc.,
and take out the ashes, etc."
And in the Gemara (Shabbos 114, beginning of amud a):
"From where do we learn changing clothes from the Torah?
As it says, 'And he shall remove,' etc."
And the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
in the clothes in which one cooked a pot for his master
he should not pour a cup for his master."
so that his fine garments not become repulsive,
in which he performs the service of eating and drinking,
such as burning offerings and pouring libations.
Accordingly it needs to be understood
why it called the important service
וְלֹא אָמַר אַל יַעֲרוֹךְ לֶחֶם לְרַבּוֹ
and did not say "he should not set bread for his master,"
which is the burning of the offerings,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר (בְּמִדְבַּר כח, ב)
in the manner of what it says (Bamidbar 28:2):
וּכְעֵין מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג ז, ב)
and similar to what is written in the holy Zohar (III 7b):
Yisrael sustain their Father in Heaven.
as with the mitzvah of sukkah (Sukkah 28b):
"like a servant who came to pour a cup for his master,
a pitcher of water on his face";
and there too a reason is needed
why the mitzvah of sukkah is compared
"so that his fine garments not become repulsive," etc.,
"and he shall remove" for taking out the ashes,
and did not command so for terumas hadeshen,
Also, why did they compare taking out the ashes
לָמָּה לֹא יִהְיֶה מִצְוַת שִׁינּוּי בְּגָדִים
why there should not be a mitzvah of changing clothes
even on weekdays when doing a mitzvah,
when one prays and puts on tefillin.
And the Maharsha, of blessed memory,
פֵּירֵשׁ הַמָּשָׁל עַל שִׁינּוּי בְּגָדִים דְּשַׁבָּת
explained the parable as referring to changing clothes for Shabbos:
in which one cooked on Erev Shabbos
that one should change when he comes
to pour the cup of Kiddush.
But even according to his explanation it is difficult:
the mitzvah of changing clothes for Shabbos
and not specifically at the time of Kiddush;
and in the Gemara (Shabbos 119a) it is explicit:
and stand at sunset of Erev Shabbos," etc.,
"Rabbi Yannai would put on his garments
so the changing of clothes is
in his commentary on the Chumash (Vayikra 6:4) wrote:
and he cited the school of Rabbi Yishmael.
from where does Rashi, of blessed memory, know
that it is not an obligation?
And at least it is a mitzvah,
since it is written explicitly in the Torah
as a command, "and he shall remove";
and it may be that it is not indispensable.
And the annotators cited Toras Kohanim;
but in Toras Kohanim there is only
(and so it is in the Gemara, Yoma 23b),
and there is no proof from this
that it is not an obligation,
in the holy Zohar, this parsha (III 33b):
"'my beloved' is none other than 'my provider,'
for through her are prepared the foods
of which it is said, 'Eat of My bread,'
and with the wine, which is the wine of Torah,
"And this is the bread of the Written Torah,
and the wine of the Oral Torah."
And this is what is said, "Eat of My bread," on the right,
"from His right hand a fiery law for them."
it is called the Written Torah,
which is 'from His right hand a fiery law for them';
and when it is taken from Gevurah
it is called the Oral Torah," etc.:
was given from the mouth of the Almighty,
and there the mighty stand in the breach.
and from the left the Oral Torah,
And as is written in Pesach Eliyahu:
we call it Torah she'b'al peh."
וְכֵן כָּתַב בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (תְּרוּמָה קסז, א)
And so it is written in the holy Zohar (Terumah, II 167a):
this is the first light, which is the right;
for from the right the left came forth";
is rooted in the Written Torah:
And it says in the holy Zohar (Terumah, II 166a)
that it explains "a mitzvah is a lamp" (Mishlei 6:23)
as the lamp, the wick and the oil
And in the Gemara (Sotah 21a) it is explicit:
"Just as a lamp gives light only for a time,
so a mitzvah gives light only for a time."
that this is not a contradiction:
only like a lamp, a wick and oil,
and without the flame it is nothing;
and this is "a mitzvah is a lamp."
which is the intent for the sake of Heaven,
and this is the "Torah is light" within the mitzvah,
and it gives light only for a time,
for learning is one of the 613 mitzvos,
lamp, wick and oil without light.
But the intent within words of Torah
is "May He open our heart through His Torah,"
and "Enlighten our eyes with Your Torah":
that the King of kings stands over him;
and the light of Torah within Torah learning
Now the actual performance of the mitzvos
מַעֲשֵׂה יָדָיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא גַּם כֵּן
the work of the hands of HaKadosh Baruch Hu as well,
as we have said several times
"in your mouth and in your heart, to do it,"
and it does not say "in your deeds":
for the completion of the deed
"whereas of the work of the hands of the tzaddikim
וְכֵן (תְּהִלִּים יט, ב) וּמַעֲשֵׂה יָדָיו וְכוּ׳
and likewise (Tehillim 19:2) "and the work of His hands," etc.:
the work of the hands of the tzaddikim,
who tells it? The firmament, etc.
שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
because HaKadosh Baruch Hu is the heart of Yisrael,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ה, ב)
שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
that HaKadosh Baruch Hu is the heart of Yisrael,
and my portion is God forever.'"
And this is what it says in the Ra'aya Mehemna
is called the letter of truth,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת וַיִּקְרָא)
as is written (holy Zohar, beginning of Parshas Vayikra):
and that is the lower Hei.
And this is what it says:
"and in your heart, to do it."

p: that this is not an obligation
by the school of Rabbi Yishmael,
he inferred that it is not an obligation.
But from the Gemara's preceding discussion
only to changing clothes on Shabbos;
and to this refers the main point of
what the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
"the Torah teaches you proper conduct," etc.
for here in Shabbos we read
"and the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught,"
which appears to refer to that;
"as the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught,"
"the Torah teaches you proper conduct" is absent.)
from the mitzvah of changing clothes
because he goes outside the camp;
which is not so of terumas hadeshen,
which is a mitzvah in the King's palace.
are compared to pouring a cup for one's master;
in which he cooked a pot for his master,
that he does for his master in the kitchen,
in them he should not pour a cup for his master,
which is service in the King's palace.
דִּכְתִיב (תְּהִלִּים צב, יד) שְׁתוּלִים בְּבֵית ה׳
as it is written (Tehillim 92:14), "planted in the house of Hashem":
is then in the house of Hashem;
he is like one to whose hand a transgression came
and he was saved from it,
since he is always accustomed to work
and he is as one who does a mitzvah,
and he is like one pouring a cup for his master
in the King's palace the whole day;
and from this there is an allusion
to changing clothes on Shabbos all day.
For the mitzvah of the Shabbos meal
that the Torah teaches you proper conduct.
But regarding taking out the ashes,
changing clothes may be a mitzvah,
since it is explicit in the Torah,
and on Shabbos it is only proper conduct,
Now the action of the mitzvah
is not called by the person's name,
but rather "the work of the hands of the tzaddikim,"
only the light of the mitzvah,
which is the intent for the sake of Heaven
this is from the person's side;
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא (עֵקֶב רעא, ב)
as is written in the Ra'aya Mehemna (Eikev, III 271b):
in one whose mind is humble;
for what is compared to water,
"Ho, all who are thirsty, go to the water,"
וְלִקְרַאת צָמֵא הֵתָיוּ מָיִם (יְשַׁעְיָה כא, יד)
and (Yeshayahu 21:14) "to meet the thirsty, bring water,"
whoever wishes may come and learn
there is not mentioned in the parable
is the actual performance of the mitzvah,
וְזֶה אֵינוֹ נִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם הָאָדָם
and that is not called by the person's name,
for the completion of the deed is from Hashem Yisbarach,
only the "Torah is light" of the mitzvah,
which is from the person's side,
is called pouring a cup for his master,
for it is the Oral Torah,
And on weekdays, when he does the mitzvah,
he is not in the King's palace,
and it is not like pouring a cup,
and he does not need to change clothes;
when he is all day in the King's palace,
he is called one who pours a cup for his master
for what he does on weekdays

p: And in the holy Zohar, this parsha
(רַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא כט, ב; נָשֹׂא קפד, ב)
the children of the King and the Queen,
are called Shabbasos and Yamim Tovim."
That is, there are talmidei chachamim
which is a day of souls
and not at all a day of the body
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב רה, א)
for they do not occupy themselves at all
with the needs of the body;
and there are some of them
who occupy themselves a little with the body's needs,
in the days of Nisan," etc.;
and nevertheless they are called Yamim Tovim,
on which work for preparing food is permitted;
וְהֵם גַּם כֵּן תָּמִיד בְּהֵיכַל הַמֶּלֶךְ
and they too are always in the King's palace,
since they do not occupy themselves
from the garments of the unlearned.
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר בְּתִקּוּנֵי זֹהַר (תִּקּוּן כא, לב, ב)
And this is what it says in Tikkunei Zohar (Tikkun 21, 32b):
"And those added to the holy people
in the palace of the King,
only that there are several holinesses.
The holiness of the camp of Yisrael,
with eating maaser sheni in Yerushalayim:
"so that you may learn to fear, etc.":
that the King of kings stands over him
And there is the holiness of the camp of the Shechinah,
וּבָהֶם יֵשׁ גַּם כֵּן כַּמָּה קְדוּשּׁוֹת
and within these too there are several holinesses:
the holiness of the Courtyard of Yisrael
and the Courtyard of the Kohanim,
and the holiness of the Holy of Holies.
are always in the King's palace;
"Show me the talmidei chachamim of Bavel,
of Rabbi Yehudah, that he resembled an angel;
who stand out like ministering angels
And it says only the talmidei chachamim of Bavel,
עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קמה, ב)
that they were not recognized in Eretz Yisrael,
like one pouring a cup for his master.
they merit the holiness of the Heichal,
the holiness of the Holy of Holies.
that in fulfilling the mitzvah of sukkah
נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן מוֹזֵג כּוֹס לְרַבּוֹ
he is also called one who pours a cup for his master,
for in the sukkah we sit
as is written in the holy Zohar, Emor (III 104a),
and he is called one who serves his master
in the palace of the King,
like one pouring a cup for his master.
"Are you more precious to us than it?")
(and as is written at the beginning of Seder Eliyahu Rabbah):
on Shabbos one becomes entirely Torah.
And he is the whole Shabbos day
like one pouring a cup for his master
and for this comes the mitzvah of changing clothes
